7c2c52f3ea:
This chapter is about where a Claude Code session gets its tools from, and how to use them well.

Half of the chapter is the Model Context Protocol. It covers the lineage (ODBC, JDBC, OSGi, the Language Server Protocol); the host, client and server roles; the JSON-RPC wire format; capability negotiation; tools, resources and prompts; the stdio and Streamable HTTP transports; and authentication. Then the practical side: the three configuration scopes and their precedence, claude mcp commands, environment-variable expansion and secrets hygiene, and the project-server approval gate. You'll build a real server with the Python SDK, see why built-in tools out-compete weak MCP descriptions, weigh community against custom servers, and measure resources as a content catalogue with a before/after.

The other half is the built-in toolbox: Grep and Glob, Read and Write, Edit and its uniqueness check, and the Read-plus-Write fallback. It includes a mini implementation of the whole set, an incremental code-exploration trace, and tracing a function through wrapper modules. Python and Java/Spring.
59b695fc67: Reading time: 3 to 3.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 19 runnable Python examples and 2 Java programs for this chapter: ccarf-companion/07-mcp-and-builtin-tools/. Run bash run_all.sh. Every example works offline, and the loop examples use the scripted fake client from chapter 01.
4f417fa50b:
The chapter rests on two sentences.

Claude Code gives the model one flat list of tools made of two kinds of entries: a fixed set of built-ins (Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, Bash and a few more) and whatever the Model Context Protocol servers you configured announced when Claude Code connected to them, and the model chooses among all of them by reading their names and descriptions.

So the job has two halves: decide which servers exist, for whom and with which secrets (scopes, .mcp.json, environment-variable expansion), make their tools and resources worth choosing (descriptions, a resource catalogue); and use the built-ins for what each does best (Grep for content, Glob for names, Read and Write for whole files, Edit for a unique targeted change, Read then Write when Edit cannot find a unique anchor).
8eb8bfe6c9:
Everything in the two task statements follows from that picture.

Servers are configured at project scope (a committed .mcp.json that every teammate receives) or at user scope (your own ~/.claude.json). That's because a tool list is something a team either shares or doesn't. Credentials never go into the committed file. The file contains ${TOKEN}, and each person's environment supplies the value.

Tools from every configured server are discovered once, at connection time. So they all sit in the model's context from the first turn, and all of them cost tokens. A tool the model has to compare with a built-in must say what it does that the built-in can't. Otherwise the better-documented built-in wins. A server can also publish read-only resources, such as a schema or a document index. Then the model reads one catalogue instead of probing the system with a dozen exploratory calls.

And the built-ins are not interchangeable. Grep and Glob answer different questions. Edit refuses an ambiguous match for a reason. And you understand a codebase one targeted search at a time, not by reading every file.
05d8fe53f7:
The official statement for 2.4 lists these knowledge points:

  • scoping at project level in .mcp.json versus user level in ~/.claude.json;
  • environment-variable expansion in .mcp.json for credentials;
  • discovery of tools from all configured servers at connection time;
  • MCP resources as a content catalogue that reduces exploratory calls.

Its skills: configure shared servers in the project file with expansion, and personal servers in the user file. Enhance MCP tool descriptions so the agent doesn't prefer built-ins. Choose community servers over custom ones for standard integrations. Expose content catalogues as resources.

For 2.5, the knowledge points are Grep for content search, Glob for path patterns, Read and Write for whole-file operations, Edit for targeted modification, and the Read-plus-Write fallback when Edit's match is not unique. The skills: choose Grep versus Glob correctly, fall back to Read then Write, build codebase understanding incrementally with targeted searches, and trace function usage across wrapper modules.

Every one of those appears below, in the order a mechanism needs them.
14bb8a231c:
Build one habit early. When an exam scenario says "the agent keeps using the wrong tool" or "the teammate cannot see the server", ask which half of the picture is broken.

  • A missing server is a configuration problem: scope, approval, a variable that isn't set.
  • A server that is present but ignored is a description problem.
  • A built-in that fails is a usage problem: a regex that needs escaping, an Edit anchor that isn't unique, a Glob used where Grep was needed.

The remedies differ, and so do the wrong answers the exam offers.
03ad74c24e: MCP is easiest to understand as the newest answer to a very old problem. How do you stop writing an adapter for every pair of things that need to talk to each other? Each earlier answer shaped a piece of what MCP does. The exam's framing ("use a standard integration instead of a custom one") only makes sense once you see why the industry kept converging on a shared protocol.
29d7d2b845:
Before 1992, a program that needed data from Oracle, Sybase, Informix and DB2 linked four vendor libraries. That meant four call conventions, four error models and four result-set APIs. Adding a database to an application meant new code in the application. Adding an application meant porting it to every database.

With N applications and M databases, the world needed up to N × M adapters. Most were written badly, because each application team knew only one database well.
6df2d634aa:
Microsoft's ODBC (1992, based on the SQL Access Group's call-level interface) put a standard API between applications and databases. It moved the vendor-specific work into a driver that the database vendor or a third party wrote once. The application called SQLConnect and SQLExecDirect, and a driver manager loaded the right driver at runtime.

JDBC (1997) did the same for Java. DriverManager.getConnection(url) picked a driver by URL. Connection, Statement and ResultSet were the same interfaces whatever sat behind them.

The arithmetic changed from N × M to N + M. Each application targets the interface once; each database ships a driver once. As a Spring developer, you've lived on the good side of that deal for twenty years. Swapping Oracle for PostgreSQL in a DataSource is a configuration change, not a rewrite.
d84d5941b9:
Notice the two ideas MCP inherits.

First, discovery by connection. The JDBC URL names the thing to connect to, and the driver reports what it can do (DatabaseMetaData lists tables, columns, supported features).

Second, capability reporting. Not every driver supports every feature, and the standard lets the client ask rather than assume.

MCP's initialize handshake and its tools/list and resources/list calls are the same two ideas, for a different kind of backend.
8cfc9717ac:
A second line of ancestry is the plug-in architecture. An application defines an extension contract and loads third-party code that satisfies it. Eclipse (2001) made this its entire personality. Its plug-ins were later formalised on OSGi, which added a module lifecycle (installed, resolved, active), a service registry where bundles publish and look up services, and the ability to add or remove a bundle without restarting the container. Browser extensions, IDE plug-ins and Spring's own auto-configuration are relatives.

The lesson MCP takes from this line is the registry of capabilities that can change at runtime. A server may add or remove tools while connected, and tells the client with a list_changed notification, much as an OSGi service registry notifies listeners.

MCP also inherits the cost, which is trust. A plug-in runs with the host's privileges. That's why Claude Code asks you before it starts a server from a committed file.
ea9a8fdf40:
By 2015 every editor (Vim, Emacs, Eclipse, Sublime) wanted code completion, go-to-definition and diagnostics for every language (Java, TypeScript, Rust, Go). That's the same N × M problem again: editors times languages.

Microsoft's Language Server Protocol (introduced with Visual Studio Code, 2016) solved it with one design choice that MCP copied almost literally. The editor and the language intelligence run as separate processes that talk JSON-RPC 2.0 over a pipe. The editor is the client, and the language server is the server. They negotiate capabilities in an initialize request ("I support rename; do you?"), then exchange requests and notifications. One Java language server works in every editor, and one editor works with every language server.

Anthropic's announcement of MCP in November 2024 described it as inspired by LSP. Read the two specifications side by side and the lifecycle sections are nearly the same shape.
4d89ef917f:
Chapter 05 traced how tool calling moved into the model API in 2023. The application declares tools in the request, the model returns a structured call, and the application runs it. That solved how a model asks for a tool. It didn't solve where tool definitions and implementations come from.

Every host application (a chat app, an IDE assistant, an agent framework) still wrote its own GitHub integration, its own Postgres integration, its own Slack integration. And every model vendor's tool-calling format was a little different. The assistant ecosystem had rebuilt the pre-ODBC world: N AI applications times M data sources and services.
c60b45f1aa:
The Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, announced November 2024 as an open standard) is the ODBC/JDBC move for that world. A server wraps a system (a database, a ticketing tool, a file store) once. It exposes that system through three standard primitives: tools, resources and prompts. A host implements the client side once and can then use any server. MCP also took LSP's process model and JSON-RPC framing, and borrowed OSGi's runtime-changing registry.

Since the announcement, other model vendors and many tools have added support. Governance of the specification has moved toward neutral stewardship under a foundation; check the current state at modelcontextprotocol.io rather than relying on this paragraph.

For the exam, hold on to the framing the task statement uses. A standard interface lets you reuse a community server for a standard system, instead of writing a custom integration.
d7784f76ae:
MCP names three roles, and exam questions use the words precisely.

  • The host is the application the user runs, which contains the model loop: Claude Code, Claude Desktop, an IDE assistant, or a program you write with the Agent SDK. The host owns the conversation, the permission prompts, and the decision of what to expose to the model.
  • The client is a protocol component inside the host that maintains one connection to one server. A host with five servers runs five client instances.
  • The server is the program that wraps a system and answers protocol requests.

When people say "I installed an MCP client", they usually mean a host. When they say "an MCP server", they mean a separate process or remote service, never something that runs inside the model.
546bf479b7:
Two properties of this arrangement matter in practice.

First, the connection is one-to-one and stateful. A client and a server negotiate once, remember what was agreed, and then exchange messages until one side disconnects. Servers don't see each other. A server never sees the conversation unless the host puts something from it into a tool argument. This is a security feature: the GitHub server can't read what the Jira server returned.

Second, the model is not a party to the protocol. The model sees tool names, descriptions and schemas that the host rendered into its context. It emits tool_use blocks in the ordinary Messages API format. The host translates a tool_use for mcp__orders__order_get_status into a tools/call request on the right client. Then it translates the server's result back into a tool_result block. From the model's side, an MCP tool and a built-in tool look the same.
9932a0d13a:
MCP messages are JSON-RPC 2.0, a tiny remote-procedure-call convention. Read it once and you'll recognise it forever. There are exactly three message shapes:

  • A request has jsonrpc, an id, a method and optional params. It expects a response with the same id.
  • A response carries either a result or an error object (with an integer code and a message), never both.
  • A notification has a method but no id, and nothing is sent back.

That's the whole mechanism. Ids correlate asynchronous replies with requests, which is why a client can have several requests in flight on one connection. Notifications carry one-way events such as "the tool list changed".
285ecfd8d3:
Compare it with what you know. A REST call is addressed by URL and verb. A JSON-RPC call is addressed by method name inside a body, and the transport carries it. A gRPC unary call has a typed request and response. JSON-RPC's params and result are untyped JSON, which the MCP specification types separately. The closest Java analogue is a JMS message with a correlation id: request/reply over a channel, with the correlation id doing the matching. Notifications are plain one-way messages.

The standard error codes come from the JSON-RPC specification: -32700 parse error, -32600 invalid request, -32601 method not found, -32602 invalid params, -32603 internal error. MCP adds a few of its own, such as -32002 for a resource that does not exist.
67c231e338:
Every MCP connection has three phases: initialization, operation and shutdown.

Initialization is where two programs that have never met decide what they can do together. It's the part that makes the protocol evolvable. The client sends an initialize request carrying the protocol version it supports, its own capabilities, and a name and version. The server answers with the version it will use, its capabilities, its name and version, and optionally an instructions string. The client then sends a notifications/initialized notification. Only then may ordinary requests begin.

Below is the exact exchange from companion example 01: a standard-library server and a hand-driven client, so there's no SDK between you and the wire. (Message framing and field names follow revision 2025-06-18 of the specification. Later revisions change details, so check the specification for the revision your SDK targets.)
08a2733030:
Read the capability objects as a contract. The server above declared tools and resources but not prompts, so a well-behaved client will never send prompts/list. It declared listChanged: false, so the client shouldn't wait for a notification that the tool list changed.

The client declared sampling (the server may ask the client's model to complete text) and roots (the client can tell the server which directories it's working in). Servers that don't need those simply ignore them.

The specification requires both sides to use only capabilities that were successfully negotiated. It's the same discipline as a JDBC driver reporting supportsBatchUpdates(). You ask first, and a "no" is an ordinary answer.
198bbcca1f:
Version negotiation is the other half of the handshake. The client sends the latest revision it supports. If the server supports that revision, it echoes it. If not, it answers with a different revision it does support, normally its latest. If the client can't speak the revision the server picked, it should disconnect.

Example 01 section 2 shows this. A client asking for the invented version 1999-01-01 gets 2025-06-18 back. Over HTTP, the client then sends the negotiated version in an MCP-Protocol-Version header on every later request.

This is why you can upgrade a server and a host independently. An old server keeps working with a new Claude Code release, because both fall back to the newest revision they share.

(Claude Code's documentation mentions that its newer MCP runtime adds a newer protocol revision. It asks servers whether they support it, and falls back otherwise. The SDK in the companion code uses that newer revision against its own client. The handshake you must understand for the exam is the shape above.)
bd9bcb2c64:
Operation is request/response plus notifications. Shutdown has no protocol message; the transport signals it. For a stdio server, the client closes the server's standard input, waits, and terminates the process if it lingers. For HTTP, it closes the connection (and may delete the session).

Two timing rules are worth knowing, because they explain real failures. Implementations should put a timeout on every request, and issue a cancellation notification when one expires. And Claude Code has startup and per-call timeouts you can raise with environment variables: MCP_TIMEOUT for startup and MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT for calls, per its documentation (check the docs for current defaults). From the host's side, a server that takes a minute to start looks exactly like a server that's broken.
a766bb64cc:
A server offers its capabilities through three primitives. The useful way to remember them is by who decides when they are used.

  • Tools are model-controlled. The model reads the list and decides to call one, as with a built-in tool.
  • Resources are application-controlled. They're read-only data identified by a URI, and the host decides how to surface them (a file-style picker, an @-mention, automatic attachment).
  • Prompts are user-controlled. They're parameterised message templates a person invokes on purpose, which Claude Code shows as slash commands.

The three share a discovery pattern: a */list call that returns names, descriptions and schemas. They also share a use pattern: tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get.
d90b544950:
A tool definition has a name, an optional human-readable title, and a description (the text the model routes on, chapter 05). It has an inputSchema in JSON Schema, an optional outputSchema, and optional annotations that hint at behaviour (read-only, destructive, idempotent).

The specification says clients must treat annotations as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. That's the right reflex: a hostile server can label a destructive tool read-only.

A call returns content, a list of typed blocks (text, image, audio, resource_link, embedded resource). It may add structuredContent, a JSON object matching the output schema. For backward compatibility, a tool that returns structured content should also return the same JSON serialised in a text block.
8b660fec3b:
There are two distinct failure channels, and chapter 06 depends on you keeping them apart.

  • A protocol error is a JSON-RPC error object: unknown tool, malformed request, server crash.
  • A tool execution error is an ordinary result whose isError is true and whose content explains what went wrong: the API timed out, the order id does not exist, the SQL was invalid.

Only the second kind is something the model can usefully reason about. So a server should report business and input problems as isError results with an actionable message, and reserve protocol errors for protocol problems. Example 01 steps 5 and 6 show the two side by side. Example 16 shows the host turning an isError result into a tool_result with is_error: true, so the model retries with a corrected id.
28a857070c:
A resource is data the server can hand over, identified by a URI: file:///project/src/main.rs, catalog://schema, order://ORD-118204.

The server lists concrete resources with resources/list (name, optional title, description, MIME type, size). It lists resource templates with resources/templates/list. These are RFC 6570 URI templates, such as catalog://runbooks/{name}, for families of resources too numerous to list. A client reads one with resources/read and gets contents as either text or base64 blob.

A server can declare subscribe (the client can ask to be told when one resource changes) and listChanged. Resources carry optional annotations: audience (user, assistant or both), priority from 0 to 1, and lastModified. A host can use these to decide what to show first or include automatically. A missing resource should produce error code -32002.
57f3ddef6b:
Why have a second primitive when a tool can return text? Because the control differs, and so does the cost model.

A tool call is a model decision that costs a round trip. A resource is something the host (or the user) can attach without a model decision. You type @orders:catalog://schema in Claude Code, and the content is attached to your message. And a resource list is a natural place for a server to say "here is everything I have, in one cheap call", before the model starts guessing. Section 17 builds a catalogue this way and measures it.
96fe1a79de:
A prompt is a named, parameterised template the server offers. triage_order(order_id) returns one or more messages with the arguments filled in. Claude Code lists them as /mcp__servername__promptname, and in the slash menu as /servername:promptname (MCP). It takes arguments space-separated after the command, and injects the result into the conversation.

A prompt is the right vehicle for a repeatable workflow that a person starts ("triage this order", "review this pull request") and that the team wants identical for everyone. It's the wrong vehicle for something the model should choose by itself. That's a tool.
6c90ff3525:
The protocol isn't one-way. A client may declare three more capabilities:

  • roots: the directories or URIs the host is working in, so a file server knows its boundary;
  • sampling: the server asks the host to run a model completion on its behalf, so a server can use a model without holding an API key;
  • elicitation: the server asks the user a structured question mid-task, and Claude Code shows a form or opens a browser for it.

These are optional and uncommon on the exam. But they complete the picture of the handshake you just read: capabilities flow in both directions.
ed4717a7dd: A transport is how the JSON-RPC messages physically travel. The specification defines two. The choice decides who runs the server, who can reach it, how it authenticates, and what can go wrong.
25c5e33af8:
With stdio, the host launches the server as a subprocess (python orders_server.py, npx -y some-mcp) and talks to it over the process's standard streams. The server reads JSON-RPC from stdin and writes JSON-RPC to stdout. Messages are separated by newlines and may not contain embedded newlines. Anything the server wants to log goes to stderr, which the host may capture, show or ignore. Starting the connection is starting the process. Ending it is closing stdin and waiting.

There's no network, no port and no authentication step. The server runs as you, with your privileges, on your machine, and trusts whoever launched it. That makes stdio the default for local tools: a filesystem server, a local database, your own scripts. It also explains why a stdio server from the internet is the same trust decision as running its code.
f8d4083430:
The one rule that bites everybody: stdout belongs to the protocol. The specification says a server must not write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message.

A print("starting") in Python corrupts the stream. So does a System.out.println in Java, a console.log in Node, or a library that writes a banner. The client's first read then fails to parse. Companion example 18 breaks it deliberately. In a host, the symptom is a server that "failed to connect" or "closed" within a second of starting, with a JSON parse error in its log.
fff9819d9b:
Streamable HTTP replaced the older HTTP-plus-SSE transport in the 2025-03-26 revision. It makes the server an independent process that can serve many clients. The server exposes one endpoint, say https://mcp.corp.example/orders, that accepts both POST and GET.

Every client message is a new POST with Accept: application/json, text/event-stream. If the body is a notification or a response, the server returns 202 Accepted with no body. If it's a request, the server chooses. It can return a single application/json body. Or it can open a text/event-stream (Server-Sent Events) response that carries progress notifications and server-initiated requests before the final response. A client must handle both. The client may also open a long-lived GET to receive server-initiated messages with no request pending.

A server may assign a session by returning an Mcp-Session-Id header on the initialize response. The client must send it on every later request. A server that requires it answers 400 when it's missing and 404 when the session has expired. At that point the client starts a new session.
b5dca54a8f:
The security rules for HTTP are not optional decoration.

  • A server must validate the Origin header on every connection. Without that check, a web page in your browser can reach a server bound to localhost through DNS rebinding.
  • A locally run server should bind to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0.
  • A server should authenticate connections.

In Claude Code you add such a server with --transport http, which is documented as the recommended transport for remote servers. The older SSE transport is still accepted but deprecated. Recent versions of Claude Code can fall back to it automatically, and a WebSocket type exists in JSON configuration. Treat those as "check the docs" details. The exam-relevant statement is simple: HTTP is for remote or shared servers, and stdio is for local processes.
39650d5079:
Authentication in MCP depends on the transport.

A stdio server has none, by design. It inherits your operating-system identity and whatever credentials you pass it, usually as environment variables in its env block.

A remote HTTP server must authenticate callers, and the specification builds that on OAuth 2.1: authorization-server discovery, PKCE, resource indicators. The details have changed between revisions, so check the authorization section of the specification for the revision you target.

From the Claude Code user's side, the flow is short. You add the server (claude mcp add --transport http jira https://mcp.atlassian.example/mcp). Then you run /mcp inside a session, choose the server and complete the browser sign-in. Or you run claude mcp login jira from the shell. Claude Code stores and refreshes the token, and "Clear authentication" in the /mcp menu discards it.

If a server uses a pre-registered OAuth client, --client-id, --client-secret and --callback-port carry those values. A fixed callback port lets the redirect URI be registered ahead of time.
8739557b28: Servers that take a static key rather than OAuth are configured with headers: --header "Authorization: Bearer ..." on the command line, or a headers object in .mcp.json. For short-lived or rotated credentials, Claude Code supports a headersHelper. That's a command that prints a JSON object of headers. It runs fresh on every connection, with a ten-second limit (per its documentation). The point of the next two sections is that the file must never contain the secret itself.
ac0a862195:
Authentication answers "who is calling?". The other half is "what may the server's output do to my agent?"

A tool result is text that goes into the model's context, and the model doesn't reliably distinguish instructions from data. A server you don't control can carry text that tries to redirect the agent. So can a server that returns content written by third parties: issue comments, web pages, support tickets.

The mitigations are the ones from chapters 03 and 05, applied to MCP:

  • permission rules that require approval for tools with side effects;
  • hooks that gate dangerous calls;
  • least-privilege tokens on the server;
  • treating tool annotations as hints, not facts.

Claude Code adds one MCP-specific lever. A server author can mark a tool with _meta["anthropic/requiresUserInteraction"] = true in the tools/list entry. Claude Code then prompts on every call. It does this even in permission modes that normally auto-approve, and even if an allow rule matches (per the documentation; it needs a recent Claude Code version).
fac9d9c0cb: Claude Code stores MCP server definitions in three places, and the location decides who sees the server. The official task statement collapses this to two ideas, project-level and user-level, because those are the two a team decision turns on. The docs name three scopes, because one more distinction is useful day to day.
039e3ad0ba:
The exam's binary framing is the one to hold: project-level .mcp.json is shared through version control; user-level ~/.claude.json is personal (and good for experimental servers you are not ready to impose on the team).

The classic scenario: "A developer configured a Jira server and it works for them, but a teammate who cloned the repo cannot see it." The configuration lives in the developer's user or local scope, which is a file on their laptop. The fix is to add it at project scope. Commit .mcp.json with credentials expressed as environment-variable references, and tell teammates which variables to set.

Example 04 reproduces the bug. A server added at user scope is missing from a teammate's resolved configuration. Re-adding it with --scope project fixes it.
9029b85ef8:
Precedence. The same server name can be defined in more than one place. The documentation lists the order, highest first: local, project, user, then plugin-provided servers, then claude.ai connectors. Claude Code connects once, using the entire entry from the highest-precedence source. Fields are not merged.

That detail causes real confusion. Say your local entry for orders points at a dev URL and has no headers. The project entry's Authorization header does not leak across, because the whole project entry is shadowed. (Servers set by an administrator in managed settings rank above all of these, in versions that support that setting.)

So the same name in two scopes is a deliberate override, not an accident to be merged. To see what is actually in force, use claude mcp list and claude mcp get <name>.
6d8c82a9dc:
A project .mcp.json is a plain file you can open, diff and review. The user and local entries live inside ~/.claude.json. That's a larger state file that Claude Code manages, and it also stores history-like data. So the right way to change those entries is the claude mcp commands, not a text editor.

The internal layout of that file is an implementation detail. The model in mcp_config.py (companion) uses projects.<path>.mcpServers for local and a top-level mcpServers for user, which matches the documented behaviour. Still, check the docs before you script against the file.
383f808d09: Configuration is normally done with claude mcp subcommands, which write the right file for the chosen scope. The forms below are the ones in the Claude Code documentation. Flags such as --scope (short -s), --transport (-t), --env (-e) and --header (-H) are repeatable where it makes sense.
c310729ba5:
Three details trip people up.

First, for stdio servers the double dash -- separates Claude's own options from the command that starts the server. Everything after it is the server's command line, so --env and --scope must come before it. The docs also note that --env can't directly precede the server name. Put another option, such as --transport stdio, between them.

Second, the default scope for claude mcp add is local, not project. A developer who runs the command without --scope project has created a server only they can see. That's exactly the "works for me" bug from the previous section.

Third, claude mcp add writes whatever you type. Paste a token into --header or --env with --scope project, and the token is now in a file you're about to commit.
1c1de24870:
A stdio entry has command, args and env. A remote entry has type (http, or sse for legacy servers) and url, plus optional headers.

A url entry without a type is a configuration error. Claude Code reads an entry with no type as a stdio server and finds no command. It skips the entry and reports that you should add "type": "http". The secrets lint in example 06 flags this too.
3dfaf967a5:
A team can share a server definition at all because the definition and the credential are different things with different audiences.

The definition is the same for everyone: where the server is, how to start it, which header name carries the token. It belongs in version control.

The credential is per person or per environment, and it must never be committed. A token in a Git history is a leaked token, even after the file is edited, and rotating it is the only real cleanup.

Environment-variable expansion lets the committed file hold the name of a variable. Each developer's shell, CI job or secrets manager supplies the value.
c0a1a32d61:
Claude Code supports two forms inside .mcp.json. ${VAR} expands to the variable's value. ${VAR:-default} uses the value if the variable is set, and the default otherwise. Expansion works in command, args, env, url and headers.

The default form is for non-secret differences, such as a base URL that a developer may point at staging. Then the file works with zero setup. Secrets get no default, because a default for a token would put a token in the file. Example 05 runs three situations through an expander:
4cebe2a747:
Read the middle case closely. It's the failure you'll actually see.

If a variable is not set and has no default, the configuration still loads. Claude Code warns and uses the literal text ${API_KEY}. The server then receives Authorization: Bearer ${API_KEY} and answers 401. The symptom looks like a bad token, not a missing variable. So the first diagnostic is "is the variable exported in the shell that launched Claude Code?", not "regenerate the token".

A related documented rule applies to remote servers. A handful of credential-bearing names (for example ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN, HTTPS_PROXY) expand to empty in url and headers, even with a default. That stops a malicious committed file from exfiltrating them to its own host. Pick your own variable names (ORDERS_TOKEN) instead of reusing those.
53b6a7346e:
The fixed file replaces each literal with a reference. It adds an .env.example that documents the variable names, which is the whole contract between the file and the people using it.

Example 06 is a pre-commit-style check you can adapt. It flags known token shapes anywhere, long opaque strings under secret-looking keys, variables that aren't documented, and the missing type.

Pair it with the usual controls: secret scanning in CI, a .gitignore for local .env files, short-lived tokens, and least privilege on the token itself. And add one habit. If a secret was ever committed, rotate it, because deleting the line doesn't delete the history.
c5be096188:
"Store the token in ~/.claude.json so it is not in the repository" is half right. It keeps the secret out of git. But it's wrong for a shared server, because teammates then have no definition at all. The expected design is a shared .mcp.json using ${VAR}, with each person providing the value.

"Commit the token in a private repository" fails too. Repositories are copied, forked, and cloned onto laptops and build servers.
dac41e8e50:
A committed .mcp.json can tell Claude Code to run any command on your machine. So a repository you just cloned from the internet could ship a "server" that is really a script.

For that reason, in interactive sessions, Claude Code asks for approval before it uses project-scoped servers from .mcp.json. claude mcp reset-project-choices clears your earlier answers. The trust model is the same as running a repository's build script: sensible for your own organisation's repositories, worth a look for anything else. Servers awaiting a decision show a "pending approval" status in claude mcp list and /mcp. Refused ones show as rejected.
f2a3625977:
Three behaviours matter for design.

Non-interactive runs cannot prompt. For claude -p, the Agent SDK and cloud sessions, the documentation says Claude Code loads project-scoped servers without asking. So a CI job that runs inside an untrusted checkout is running whatever that checkout's .mcp.json says. You have three ways to keep a server out regardless of mode. List it in disabledMcpjsonServers, which blocks it in every permission mode. Restrict which setting sources are read. Or start with --strict-mcp-config, so only servers passed with --mcp-config are used.

A repository cannot approve itself. Settings keys such as enableAllProjectMcpServers and enabledMcpjsonServers pre-approve servers. But when they're committed in a project's .claude/settings.json, they're ignored in a folder you haven't marked trusted (documented from version 2.1.196; check the docs).

Organisations can constrain the whole mechanism with managed settings, which sit above every other scope.
4a51457a61:
When a session starts, Claude Code resolves the configuration, creates a client for each server, and runs the initialization handshake. For each server that advertised the tools capability, it calls tools/list, following nextCursor if the list is paged. It does the same for resources and prompts. The result is merged into the catalogue the model sees. MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>, so two servers that both export search don't collide.

The exam says "tools from all configured servers are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously". It means exactly this: no per-request selection of servers, no lazy loading by default in the protocol, and no server-by-server mode. If five servers are configured and connected, the model can call any tool of any of them from the first turn.
7fc06ab319:
Two consequences follow, and the chapter 05 cost model applies to both.

The first is context cost. Every definition (name, description, schema) is input tokens on every request. Example 03 connects the real orders server and a second small server. It finds seven MCP tools costing about 765 input tokens on every request, in the companion's rough estimate. A real server like a project tracker can export dozens of tools. Several such servers can eat a large part of the context window before the user has typed anything.

The second is choice noise. More tools mean more near-neighbours to confuse.
7c9086674d:
Claude Code has several mechanisms that bend the "everything is loaded up front" picture. A careful answer mentions that they exist, without assuming they're on.

  • Tool search (documented as enabled by default for supported models) defers MCP tool definitions. Only tool names and server instructions load at session start, and the model searches for definitions when it needs them. ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH can force it off or switch to a threshold mode. A server can be exempted with alwaysLoad: true in its configuration.
  • Descriptions and server instructions are truncated at 2,048 characters per tool by default. So critical routing information belongs at the start.
  • Claude Code checks each tool's input schema when it loads a server. It excludes a tool whose schema would make the API reject the whole request (for example, property names outside the allowed character set), and tells the model which tool was excluded and why.
  • Servers can change their lists at runtime with list_changed notifications. Claude Code applies these without a reconnect in interactive sessions.

All of those are version-dependent. The stable exam knowledge is the default model: discover at connection, list everything, name by prefix.
cf9d867760:
Understanding a server from the inside removes most of the mystery from the protocol. The official Python SDK has a high-level server class that turns decorated Python functions into protocol definitions. It's named FastMCP in the 1.x line and MCPServer in 2.x; the companion code imports whichever is installed.

The mapping is the thing to learn:

  • the function name becomes the tool name;
  • the docstring becomes the description the model routes on;
  • type hints (and pydantic.Field constraints) become the inputSchema;
  • the return value becomes the result content (and structured content for typed returns);
  • an exception becomes an isError result.

So everything chapter 05 said about descriptions applies to docstrings. A function with no docstring is published with an empty description.
fe35c31df1: Below is the heart of orders_server.py from the companion: two lookup tools, a SQL tool, a resource that serves the schema catalogue, a resource template for runbooks, and a prompt. The tool docstrings follow the eight-part pattern from chapter 05 (purpose, use-when, not-for, return, edge case). They also include the sentence this chapter is about: they say when to prefer this tool over reading files or running generic queries.
88057d13aa:
Run example 02 and you see what a client sees. There are five tools with their parameters and first description lines, two resources, one resource template and one prompt, plus the server instructions.

The same file answers a bad call the way a good tool should. Calling order_get_status with "bad" fails schema validation. It comes back as a result with is_error true and a message naming the pattern. Example 16 later feeds that same shape back to the model for a retry.
b14038d51b: A stdio server in the repository is shared by committing the file that launches it. The server code lives in the repo (tools/orders_server.py). The launch definition lives in .mcp.json, and the secrets live in environment variables.
9adeee6c7d:
Each teammate then needs the Python dependencies installed and the variable exported. The first time they open the repository, Claude Code asks them to approve the server.

For a server shared across many repositories, deploy it once as a Streamable HTTP service with OAuth, and give everyone the same two-line definition. In the Agent SDK, the same server is configured in code through the mcp_servers option of ClaudeAgentOptions. Its tools are allowed with the same mcp__orders__... strings (check the SDK reference for the current option shape).
1efd6c9695:
A Spring service already has what an MCP tool needs: a typed method, validated input and a result. The mapping is mechanical.

  • A @Service method with a record parameter is a tool.
  • The record's bean-validation annotations (@Pattern(regexp = "^ORD-\d{6}$")) are the inputSchema constraints.
  • The Javadoc or an annotation attribute is the description.
  • A thrown OrderNotFoundException mapped to isError is a tool execution error.

There are official and community Java SDKs for MCP, and a Spring AI integration that exposes annotated beans as tools. Check the Spring AI and MCP Java SDK documentation for the current annotations; don't rely on names from memory.

The design rule transfers untouched: the description is the contract the model reads. Write it in the user's vocabulary, and say when not to use the tool. Section 21 shows a Java version of the Edit check, and the companion adds a Java scope resolver.
233580f274:
The task statement lists a skill that sounds odd until you've watched it happen: enhance MCP tool descriptions to prevent the agent from preferring built-in tools.

The mechanism is the one from chapter 05. The model has no router, only text. Claude Code's built-in tools arrive with long, careful descriptions, tuned over many releases, with strong examples. Grep says what it's for, what syntax it uses, and when to use it instead of shell commands. An MCP server written in an afternoon often arrives with "Search code." or an empty docstring.

When a request could be served by either, the model compares what it's told. The better-explained, familiar tool wins, even when the MCP tool is objectively better for the job (it's indexed, it spans repositories, it knows ownership). The symptom is a team that installs a code-search server and watches the agent keep running Grep.
8488d58e14:
A prompt that says "always use code_search" is not the fix. Chapter 05 showed how absolute instructions bias selection and leak into unrelated requests. The fix is a description that does three jobs:

  • It says what this tool can do that the built-in cannot: semantic search, other repositories, generated code, owners.
  • It says in the user's vocabulary when to choose it ("where do we retry payments across all repositories").
  • It says when to hand the request back to the built-in ("for an exact string inside the current working tree prefer Grep"). That keeps the model from over-correcting.

Example 09 uses an offline bag-of-words scorer as a stand-in for the model and routes eight requests two ways. It isn't Claude; as in chapter 05, it shows the mechanism.
2fb398a525: When tool search is on, only names and server instructions are loaded up front. That raises the value of two things. One is the server instructions field, which tells the model when to go looking for your tools. The other is descriptive, namespaced tool names, because search matches against them. Both are cheap to improve, and both are in your control as the server author.
487dfcde92:
The exam skill is stated plainly: choose existing community MCP servers over custom implementations for standard integrations. The reasoning is the N + M arithmetic from section 02, applied to your own team.

GitHub, Jira, Slack, PostgreSQL, Sentry, Google Drive, a filesystem and a browser are standard systems with public APIs. Several have official servers published by the vendor, or well-maintained community servers. Write your own and you own the pagination bugs, the OAuth flow, the rate-limit handling, the schema drift when the vendor changes the API, and the security review. You gain nothing over code that other people already exercise daily.

A custom server is justified in three cases. The system is specific to you (the proprietary order platform, the internal pricing engine). The existing server doesn't expose what you need. Or your security model forbids third-party code in the path.
ff1d2a5d8c:
"Prefer community servers" does not mean "install whatever you find." A server runs with your credentials, and its output goes into your agent's context. Treat adoption like adopting a library:

  • prefer vendor-published or widely used servers;
  • read what scopes the token needs, and give it the least;
  • pin a version rather than floating on latest;
  • read the tool list for write operations you don't want, and deny them with permission rules;
  • wrap or fork only when the gap is real.

A reasonable pattern is to adopt a community server for the standard system and add a thin custom server on top for your internal conventions. Its descriptions tell the model which one to use when. (For discovery, the Claude Code ecosystem includes registries of servers; check the docs for what your version offers.)
a12b8e6ed5:
Every MCP tool the model sees is named mcp__<server>__<tool>: mcp__orders__order_get_status. The host composes the prefix from the server name in your configuration and the tool name from tools/list. That's why server names matter beyond cosmetics. Characters in the server name that aren't letters, digits, underscore or hyphen are replaced when the name is built (the exact rule is a docs detail; example 08 models it).

The prefix makes names unique, not different. mcp__kb__search and mcp__orders__search both still say "search" to the model. That's why chapter 05 told you to name the server for the system it fronts, and the tool for the operation.
21103a6d9b:
Permission rules, hook matchers and subagent tool lists all use these strings. In permission rules, mcp__orders matches any tool of the server. mcp__orders__* does the same with a wildcard. mcp__orders__order_get_status matches one tool.

Allow rules may glob only after a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix. So mcp__github__get_* is accepted, but a bare mcp__* or * in an allow list is skipped with a warning and approves nothing. Deny and ask rules may use broader patterns, and deny always wins over allow at every level.

Rules containing parentheses on an mcp__ tool are skipped, because MCP rules don't match on arguments. To block a specific argument pattern, you use a hook. In the Agent SDK, allowed_tools and disallowed_tools take the same strings.
6fdffbaafd:
Three practical points.

Deferral and rules both key on names. So a naming scheme with a shared verb prefix (get_, list_ for reads; create_, delete_ for writes) lets you allow reads with one glob and ask on writes with another.

Plugin-bundled servers use a different prefix form (the docs show mcp__plugin_<plugin>_<server>__<tool>). A hook matcher written for mcp__database-tools__.* won't fire for one.

And a server's prompts become /mcp__server__prompt commands using the same normalised server name. So renaming a server renames everything downstream of it: rules, hooks, commands, and your team's muscle memory.
c318c284d5:
An agent that meets an unfamiliar system has to learn its shape before it can do useful work. A tool-only server lets it learn in only one way: by probing. List the tables, describe each table, sample a few rows, guess a column, fail, correct. Each probe is a model round trip, with latency, tokens, and another chance to wander. And the knowledge gained is private to that conversation.

A content catalogue published as an MCP resource inverts this. The server's author knows the system, and writes one document that says what exists and how it fits together. That might be tables with their columns, keys and meaning; the document index of a knowledge base; the issue categories of a tracker; or the service map of a platform. The agent (or the user, with an @-mention) reads it once and then acts directly.
29ce9c43ac:
This is the skill the task statement names: expose content catalogues as MCP resources to reduce exploratory tool calls. It's a design pattern with three parts.

  1. Publish a top-level catalogue resource with a stable URI (catalog://schema), whose description says "read this first".
  2. Back it with templated detail resources (catalog://runbooks/{name}, order://{id}) for drilling down.
  3. Put the pointer where the model will see it: in the server instructions field, and in the descriptions of the exploratory tools ("prefer reading catalog://schema"), as orders_server.py does.

A resource nobody mentions is a resource nobody reads.
96d411f756:
Example 10 runs two deterministic policy agents against the real server. Both answer the same five warehouse questions ("which small-business accounts have an order waiting on a port-in?", "total order value by segment", and so on).

The explorer has no catalogue. For each question it lists the tables and describes every table it needs. In two of the five, it first guesses a column name wrong and retries after the error. The catalogue agent reads catalog://schema once and writes each query directly.

The policies are scripted to be plausible, not measured from a model, so the absolute numbers are illustrative. The shape is the point. Your own tracing will tell you the ratio.
775036b559: Include names, one-line meaning, keys and joins, enumerations of valid values, units, and pitfalls ("shipments is empty until the order ships"). That's what stops the wrong-column guess.
718ed5eb02: Keep it small. A catalogue is read into the context. A 40,000-token dump of every column of every table just moves the exploration problem into one call. Put the overview in the top resource and the long tail behind templates.
b9b26f3fb6: Make it current. Generate it from the source of truth (the database metadata, the OpenAPI document) instead of writing it by hand. If it changes while sessions are open, publish listChanged or subscription notifications.
c6f85d1f62:
How does the user reach resources in Claude Code? Typing @ lists resources from connected servers alongside files. The form @server:protocol://path references one (for example @docs:file://api/authentication). Referenced resources are fetched and attached automatically.

Claude Code also provides tools to list and read MCP resources, so the model can read a catalogue itself. The exact tool names are a host detail; ask Claude in a session what resource tools it has, or check /mcp. Resources whose URI starts with ui:// are UI pages for a host application, not content for the model, and aren't offered in the @ menu.

Prompts, the third primitive, appear as slash commands. /mcp__orders__triage_order ORD-118205 runs the server's triage template.
ea18b68239:
If the model should decide to fetch it, and it may take arguments that change the answer, it's a tool. If it's stable reference material that a person or the host could just as well attach, it's a resource.

"List all tables" is the classic mistake. It's reference material, and as a tool it costs a round trip every session. Keep the exploratory tools as a fallback, and say in their descriptions to prefer the resource.
0d30865cd4:
Task statement 2.5 is about choosing the right built-in tool. The way to choose is to know the contract of each one. The contracts differ in exactly the dimensions that cause failures:

  • what the tool matches on (names or content);
  • what it returns (paths, lines, counts, the whole file);
  • whether it changes anything;
  • what it requires first.

Claude Code's tools reference lists the full set. These are the ones the exam and daily work revolve around.
35b24b1844:
Notice that the table is organised by the question, not the tool. Grep and Glob are both "search" in everyday speech, and both read-only, which is why people confuse them. They differ in what they look at. Read and Write are both whole-file operations. Edit is the targeted variant of Write.

The remaining tools (WebFetch, WebSearch, NotebookEdit, the subagent tool and so on) aren't part of the objective. They follow the same pattern of tool name, description and schema that you've been reading since chapter 05.
790a184ea4:
Here's a current detail worth knowing, so a real session doesn't surprise you. The Claude Code documentation says that on macOS, Linux and WSL, Glob and Grep may be left out of the default tool set. Claude then searches through the Bash tool instead, using embedded find-compatible and grep-compatible commands. The tools return when you name them in --tools or --allowedTools, when Bash is removed, or when a subagent lists them. On Windows they're part of the default set.

This is a distribution detail that changes between releases (check the docs for your version). It doesn't change the exam model. The objective is the distinction between searching content and matching paths. That distinction holds whether the tool is called Grep or is a grep command.
b677ed276e:
Grep searches what is inside files; Glob matches what files are called. That sentence resolves almost every exam question on the subject.

To find where charge_card is used, look at file contents, because that's where the function name appears. No filename contains it, so Glob("**/*charge_card*") returns nothing, and Grep is the tool. To list every test file, the information is in the path (tests/test_*.py). Glob answers in one call. A Grep for def test_ would return lines you didn't ask for.

A useful two-question rule: do I know part of a path and want files? Glob. Do I know text inside files and want lines or files containing it? Grep.

Example 13 runs eight realistic requests through the rule. Then it runs the wrong tool on each, so you can see what a mistake returns: usually nothing (Glob for content) or plausible noise (Grep for names).
a2d8054804: The silent failure is the dangerous one. A Glob for a function name returns "no files found". An agent that trusts that result concludes the function doesn't exist or is unused. That's a confident wrong answer, built on a correct tool run for the wrong question. Treat an empty result as "this tool could not have seen it" before you treat it as "it is not there".
61d0cd0435:
Claude Code's Grep is built on ripgrep and uses ripgrep's regular-expression syntax, not POSIX grep. So metacharacters need escaping: searching Go code for interface{} takes the pattern interface\{\}. A pattern ripgrep rejects returns an error with ripgrep's diagnostic, so the model can fix it. Example 11 shows a mini version: regex parse error: missing ), unterminated subpattern.

Three output modes shape the result, and therefore the context cost:

  • files_with_matches is the default. It returns paths only, the cheapest way to answer "where".
  • content returns matching lines with file and line number, optionally with context lines, for "show me".
  • count returns matches per file plus a total, for "how widespread".

You can narrow results with a glob filter (**/*.tsx) or a type (py, rust), limit them with head_limit, and make them multi-line with multiline: true. Grep skips files excluded by .gitignore. To search an ignored file, pass its path directly.
55fe936f0d:
Glob supports standard glob syntax, with ** for recursive directories (src/**/*.ts, *.{json,yaml}). It returns paths sorted by modification time. It's capped at 100 files, with a truncation flag so the model knows to narrow the pattern.

It does not respect .gitignore by default, so it finds ignored build output that Grep would skip. Example 11 shows this asymmetry. Glob("build/*") returns build/out.txt, while Grep("build artifact") reports no matches in the same file. The asymmetry is a frequent source of "the tools disagree" confusion. The documented environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_GLOB_NO_IGNORE controls it (check the docs for the value semantics in your version).
31b4660766: The cheap way to locate and the expensive way to understand fit together. First, use Grep in files_with_matches mode to find which files matter. Then use content mode with a narrow path or glob to see the lines. Then Read the surrounding function, with offset and limit if the file is long. Each step narrows the next, and the context only ever holds what the next decision needs. Section 22 puts numbers on this.
c013a19f41:
Edit is exact string replacement. It takes a file_path, an old_string and a new_string (and an optional replace_all). It finds old_string in the file and replaces it. It doesn't use regular expressions, and it doesn't fuzzy-match. A single character of whitespace or indentation difference is a miss.

The documentation lists three checks that must pass before an edit applies.

  • Read-before-edit: the model must have read the file in the current conversation. A read cut short by a "PARTIAL view" notice does not count. Newer models can relax this in some cases, and viewing the file with certain read-only Bash commands also satisfies it.
  • Match: old_string must appear in the file exactly as written.
  • Uniqueness: old_string must appear exactly once. If it appears more than once, the model must either supply a longer string with enough surrounding context to pin down one occurrence, or set replace_all: true to replace all of them.
6c96a2a6cf:
Why is uniqueness a rule, instead of "replace the first one"? Because a replace-first rule would make Edit silently wrong whenever the model's mental picture of the file disagreed with the file.

Consider timeout = 30, which appears in three functions. A model that asks to change it to 60 almost certainly means one of them. Replacing the first would change the wrong function and report success. Refusing the ambiguous request forces the model to say which one by including context. That's the only way the edit can be correct.

It's the same principle as a database UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? that must hit exactly one row. It's also why an optimistic-locking version check exists. An operation that is specific about its target fails loudly instead of corrupting quietly.
360bb74ce2: Example 12 uses a file whose three functions each contain timeout = 30. It asks for refund_card's timeout, and only that one, to become 60. The mini Edit in the companion reproduces the contract. Its messages are modelled on the real ones, not copied; run the real tool to see yours.
23d4d6ca1d:
Case A is a drift problem. The text the model remembers isn't the text on disk: a tab, a trailing space, a line that changed since the read. The remedy is to Read again and copy the exact text.

Case B is the ambiguity this section is about.

Case C is the right fix when a short unique anchor exists. Include enough neighbouring lines that the string occurs once.

Case D is correct only when the intent really is "all of them", such as renaming a variable throughout a file. Otherwise it's dangerous. Here it changes three timeouts when one was wanted.

Case E is the fallback.
d017cb8269:
When Edit can't find a unique anchor, the task statement says to Read the file, then Write it back with the change. The situations that call for it are those where no short, unique substring exists, or where the change isn't local:

  • highly repetitive generated files, where every candidate anchor repeats;
  • a restructuring that touches many scattered places that must stay consistent;
  • a file whose whitespace is irregular enough that exact matching keeps failing;
  • replacing most of the file anyway.

The procedure is exactly two steps. Read the whole file, so the model has the true current text (and so the read-before-write rule is satisfied). Write the full corrected content.

Write replaces the entire file, so anything the model omitted is deleted. That's why the Read must be complete (not a PARTIAL view), and why the fallback is not the default. It trades Edit's precision for generality, and it costs output tokens proportional to the whole file.
2ae621c6de:
Write creates a new file, or overwrites an existing one, with exactly the content given. It doesn't append or merge.

For overwrites, the documentation says older models always require a prior Read of the file in the conversation. Newer models can overwrite an unread file only under the same conditions as read-before-edit. Notebooks and partially read files always require the read. Creating a new file has no such requirement. For a partial change to an existing file, the guidance is to use Edit, not Write.

Example 12 ends with "Write without Read" refused, for exactly this reason. The rule protects against the opposite failure from Edit's. The danger here isn't changing the wrong occurrence. It's overwriting content you never saw.
ef05f8c72c:
The fastest way to stop being surprised by these tools is to write them. mini_tools.py in the companion is about 150 lines. It implements Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep against a working directory, with the documented contracts:

  • numbered Read output, and a PARTIAL notice for long files;
  • Write that refuses to overwrite an unread file;
  • Edit that checks read-before-edit, then match, then uniqueness, against the current file content;
  • Glob that ignores .gitignore, sorts by modification time and caps at 100;
  • Grep that honours .gitignore, has three output modes, and returns regex errors as errors.

It isn't the real implementation. It's the same shape: a function per tool, a JSON schema, a dispatcher, and every outcome converted to text the model can read. The core of Edit is a dozen lines.
034bc3e748:
Note the two things the return value is: a string and an error flag. The flag becomes is_error on the tool_result block. The string is what the model reads next.

That design is why the failure messages above matter. The message for ambiguity names both ways out (replace_all or more context), so the model's next call is predictable. A tool whose error said only "edit failed" would force a guess. This is chapter 06's "errors as information", applied to a built-in.
49015f5bb1:
Companion program java/EditTool.java (JDK 17 single-file) reproduces the check order in Java, with a record Result(boolean ok, String message) as the return type.

The only language-specific care is that String.replaceFirst takes a regular expression. A literal old_string containing { or . would misbehave unless quoted. The program wraps it in Pattern.quote and Matcher.quoteReplacement. That's the Java form of the Grep escaping rule from section 19: the tool is literal, but the library underneath is not.
aaf7061c3e:
The task statement's phrase is build codebase understanding incrementally rather than reading all files upfront. The failure it prevents is the instinct to "get oriented" by opening everything.

In a real repository that's impossible, because the files don't fit. It's wasteful, because most are irrelevant. And it's harmful: the context fills with noise that later turns must carry, and the answer you need gets diluted.

The incremental method treats exploration as a series of cheap questions. Each is answered by the narrowest tool that can answer it, and the result of one question decides the next.
0fe1d9744a: The sample repository in the companion has 45 files: a billing package, an orders package, an API layer, a nightly job, tests, two config files, and 30 generated stubs that add bulk. The question is "where is the gateway timeout set, and is it the same in staging and prod?". Example 14 answers it twice.
a655785b8a:
Look at what each step contributed.

The first Grep returned three paths in 14 tokens. It told the agent the term lives in config/ and src/billing/, and nowhere in the API, jobs or orders code.

The second and third Greps, scoped by path, returned the actual lines. From them the answer was almost complete: two YAML files each with timeout: 30, and three timeout = 30 assignments in gateway.py.

The final Read confirmed the one fact the lines couldn't: that the code assigns a constant rather than reading configuration.

The 4 percent figure is for a 45-file toy. On a real repository the gap is larger, because the read-everything strategy doesn't terminate. But even here it shows the direction. It also shows the order of the loop: locate (Grep, files only) → view (Grep, content, narrow) → understand (Read a slice) → decide the next question.
961fc8cc04: Start with the cheapest question that narrows the space. A Glob of the top-level layout, or a files_with_matches Grep for the term, costs tens of tokens. It removes most of the repository from consideration.
1d346501b6: Widen only when a result says so. If the first Grep hits nothing, change the term before changing the strategy. Try synonyms, the config key instead of the code symbol, or a different casing.
7c525d67a7: Keep a running hypothesis in the agent's visible reasoning or a scratch note. The next search is chosen to confirm or kill it.
2f0cac6d30: The Explore subagent from chapter 02 is the same method, with isolation. It does the searching in its own context and returns a summary, so even the narrow search results don't accumulate in the main conversation. For a large, unfamiliar area, delegating the exploration is the incremental method taken one level up.
ad99821249:
The last skill in 2.5 is trace function usage across wrapper modules by first finding all exported names, then searching for each name across the codebase.

The trap is that code changes names on its way up. Follow one chain:

  • a function charge_card is called by a retry helper charge_with_retry;
  • a package __init__ re-exports that helper under the friendlier name charge;
  • two modules import it, one as from billing import charge and one as billing.charge(...);
  • one of their callers is aliased again in a legacy module as place_order.

A search for the original name finds the first link in the chain and nothing else. Say you're about to change charge_card's signature. "One caller" is the wrong answer; the blast radius is the whole chain.
c3ff45b347:
The method is a loop, and it's mechanical enough to write down. Search a name. Classify each hit. Collect any new names. Repeat for each new name until no new names appear.

A hit is one of these:

  • the definition (ignore);
  • a call (the new name is the enclosing function, so the chain continues upward);
  • a rename, either import X as Y or an assignment Y = module.X (the new name is Y);
  • an import without rename (no new name, but it tells you which files depend on the module);
  • a comment or string (ignore, but note it as stale);
  • noise, such as an unrelated dictionary key that happens to share the word.

Example 15 runs the loop with the mini Grep tool against the sample repository.
e42e624955:
Several habits make the trace reliable.

  • Start from the exported surface when a package re-exports. Read the package's __init__ (or the Java module's public API) first. It tells you which names the outside world uses, and which internal names are aliased.
  • Anchor searches with word boundaries (\bcharge\b), so charge_card and discharge don't match. Add shape (charge\(, import .* charge) when a name is generic, as charge is.
  • Read the ambiguous hits. The "charge" dictionary key in refund_card is a legitimate regex hit, not a use of the function. Only reading the line tells you.
  • Do not trust names alone where the language allows dynamic dispatch, reflection or string-based wiring: Spring beans referenced by name in XML, Python getattr, plugin registries. Grep for the string forms too, and say so when the trace can't be complete.
  • Grep the tests. They're callers too, and often the only ones for rarely used paths.
4494c354f8:
You'll know the Java version of this problem. In a Spring codebase, "who calls PaymentGateway.charge()?" passes through an interface, a Spring proxy, an @Async wrapper, and perhaps a Feign client. The IDE's "find usages" resolves the type hierarchy. A text search sees only names.

A text-search agent compensates by searching for the interface name, the implementation name, bean names in configuration, and the method name qualified by receiver. It's the same loop, run over more kinds of alias.

Claude Code can use a language-server tool for type-aware navigation where one is configured (the tools reference documents an LSP tool; check the docs for availability). When it does, you get semantic usages instead of textual ones. The exam asks about the text-search technique because that's what the built-ins provide.
b8a50badbb:
To see both halves of the chapter work together, example 16 runs a scripted model through a single loop. Its catalogue contains the five file tools, five MCP tools from the real orders server, and a resource reader.

The host code routes each tool_use by its name. Names starting mcp__orders__ go to the MCP connection with the prefix stripped. The resource reader calls resources/read. Everything else goes to the mini file tools. The scenario is "order ORD-118205 failed overnight settlement; why, and where is the job code?".
5f598bbb5e:
Four things in this trace are worth noticing.

  • The first call fails with a validation error from the MCP server, which the host returns as is_error: true. The message names the expected pattern, so the model's second call succeeds. That recovery is the chapter 06 pattern, running through MCP.
  • The runbook came from a resource template, not a tool. No model-controlled lookup tool was needed for static reference text.
  • The code search used Grep, because the question was about a symbol's text. The file view used Read once the path was known.
  • The whole investigation used six model calls and no exploratory probing, because each step's output named the next step.

(The reader tool's name in this scripted loop is illustrative. Claude Code provides its own resource-listing and resource-reading tools, whose names you can see with /mcp or by asking.)
a952433d35:
One last MCP practicality sits between the two task statements: how big can a result be?

The Claude Code documentation gives defaults. It warns when an MCP tool result exceeds 10,000 tokens. It truncates at 25,000 tokens, which you can raise with MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS. Text over 50,000 characters is saved to a file, and a tool can raise its own threshold through result metadata, up to a stated maximum. Verify the exact numbers for your version.

The built-ins have their own limits. Read returns a PARTIAL view for a whole-file read that exceeds the token limit, and expects offset and limit for more. Bash output beyond roughly 30,000 characters is saved to a file with a preview. Glob caps at 100 paths.

In every case, a truncated or file-parked result is something the model can't reason about. So the design response is the same on both sides of the objective. Cap rows, return a cursor and a total, offer filters, and tell the model in the result how to ask for the next page.
e5164471e1:
Almost every mechanism in this chapter has a Spring counterpart you already use. Mapping them is faster than memorising them.

Scopes are Spring's property-source hierarchy. A committed application.yml plays the project .mcp.json. A developer's ~/.config/spring-boot/application-local.yml or an @TestPropertySource plays user and local scope. And there's an override order in which the more specific source wins.

Like Spring's property sources, Claude Code resolves a name to one winning definition. The difference: Spring merges individual keys across sources by default, and Claude Code doesn't merge fields inside a server entry. Remember that when an override seems to "lose" a header.

Environment-variable expansion is the ${ORDERS_TOKEN} and ${orders.url:https://default} placeholder syntax from @Value and application.yml. The syntax differs by a character: Spring's default separator is :, and Claude Code's is the shell-style :-. The idea is identical, and so is the rule: secrets get no default.
258937e97d:
Discovery at connection time is JDBC's DatabaseMetaData and Spring's classpath scanning. You ask the provider what it has, once, when you connect.

The catalogue resource is the OpenAPI document or the Actuator /actuator/mappings endpoint: a machine-readable index that spares clients from probing.

The approval gate is the dependency-trust problem of running someone else's build plugin. enableAllProjectMcpServers in an untrusted folder is the equivalent of a malicious pom.xml plugin. That's why it isn't honoured there.

Tool names and permission rules resemble Spring Security's method-level rules (@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('orders:read')")): a naming convention that doubles as an access-control vocabulary.

And Edit's uniqueness check is an UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? that must touch exactly one row. Read plus Write is the fallback of loading the aggregate, changing it in memory, and saving the whole thing.
f07025f57a: Configuration problems are the most common real-world MCP failures, and a favourite exam theme. So keep the diagnostic order in your head. Work from "is it defined?" to "is it trusted?" to "does it start?" to "is it chosen?".
a82bc4c32b: Is it defined where you think? claude mcp list and claude mcp get <name> show what is in force, and from which scope. A server missing for a teammate is almost always in user or local scope on your machine (section 08). A server that exists but behaves differently from the file in git is being shadowed by a higher-precedence entry of the same name.
2c18ba1614: Is the entry valid? Some entries are skipped with a message rather than loaded half-way: a url without type, a stdio entry without command, or an sdk-type entry (only SDK hosts can register those).
6c7b688744: Is it approved? A project server shows "pending approval" until the developer accepts it. It shows "rejected" if it was refused or listed in disabledMcpjsonServers. In an untrusted folder, committed settings can't approve it (section 11).
9085883b1e: Did the variables expand? An unset ${VAR} with no default doesn't stop loading. It sends the literal text, and the server answers 401 or fails to start. Export the variable in the shell that launches Claude Code, and restart (section 10).
9754628a61: Does the process start and speak clean stdio? Run the command by hand. A banner on stdout, a missing dependency, a wrong working directory, or a slow start that exceeds the startup timeout all look like "failed to connect" (sections 06 and 04). Raise MCP_TIMEOUT only once you know the server is merely slow.
e30006dfa4: Is the tool visible, and is it chosen? /mcp lists each server's tools. If the tool is listed but never used, the problem has moved from configuration to description (section 14). If a tool is missing from a connected server, check two things: a schema Claude Code excluded as invalid, or tool search deferring it until the model looks for it.
1793febb07: Is a permission rule in the way? A deny rule, or an unanchored allow glob that was skipped, changes whether the call runs without a prompt. That's easy to mistake for the tool not working (section 16).
371f80b613: Each anti-pattern below looks reasonable, fails in a specific and predictable way, and has a small fix. The code is from the companion. The fixes are what the exam rewards.
d5cbb54d73: Failure trace: the token is in Git history. A leaked clone gives the holder access to the orders API. Deleting the line later doesn't remove it from history. The fix is three things together: the reference, rotation of the exposed token, and a secret scanner in CI.
c37774097c: Failure trace: the next developer who clones the repository has no jira in claude mcp list. They file an "MCP is broken" ticket, yet nothing is wrong with MCP. Example 04 reproduces this.
725c23edaa: Failure trace: with double quotes, your shell replaces the placeholder with the token from your own environment. The command then writes that token into the file you're about to commit. The linter in example 06 catches the result. The habit that prevents it: open the generated file and read it before git add.
c4aae206a0: Failure trace: the team pays for an indexed search service, and the agent keeps running Grep because Grep is the better-documented tool. Adding "ALWAYS use code_search" to the system prompt pulls exact-string questions to the wrong tool as well. Fix the description instead (section 14).
85b0bc76d3: Failure trace: the loop repeats the same failing call. Or worse, the model reaches for replace_all and changes all three timeouts. The error text names both ways out, and the right choice depends on intent.
90e470a4fd: As in earlier chapters, the wrong options are sound practices applied at the wrong layer. Decide before you read the reasoning. For each question, name which half of the picture it's about: configuration, description or usage.
0b00658c5e:
The command without --scope used the default local scope. That lives in the developer's ~/.claude.json and isn't shared. Project scope writes a committed .mcp.json that every clone receives, and the approval prompt is the trust step.

A works once, but it isn't a team configuration and it will drift. C shares someone's whole personal state file, including unrelated servers and tokens. D confuses memory with configuration. CLAUDE.md holds instructions, not server definitions, so no server would start.
2de9f78479:
Environment-variable expansion exists so the committed file holds the variable name, and each person supplies the value.

A leaks the token to everyone with clone access, and into history. B works for one person but defeats sharing: new teammates have no definition at all. D is encoding, not protection, because base64 is trivially reversible.

Remember the documented behaviour when a variable is unset. The file still loads and the literal text is sent. So on a 401, the first thing to check is whether the variable is exported.
7de6dda46b:
This is a description problem. The model picks the better-explained tool, and Grep's description is much stronger. B gives the model the information it needs to choose correctly, and hands back to Grep the cases Grep is better at.

A is the absolute-instruction pattern. It biases unrelated requests and ignores the root cause. C removes a tool that's right for most single-repository questions, and still leaves a weak description. D changes a name, not the information in it.
4aece12506:
A resource catalogue lets the agent (or the user, with @) learn the shape of the system in one read. That removes the list/describe/guess/retry steps. Templates keep the long tail out of the main document.

A addresses output length, not the probing. C merges contracts and makes failures harder to diagnose. D would work for a tiny static schema. But it goes stale, duplicates what the server knows, and puts 60 tables into every session whether they're needed or not. Generate the catalogue from the database metadata.
cec56ae847:
Edit refuses an ambiguous match so that it can't silently change the wrong place. The remedies are to make the anchor unique with context, or, when no such anchor exists, to fall back to Read then Write.

A repeats a deterministic failure. B changes all three and then needs manual repair, the opposite of a targeted edit. D uses a path-matching tool for a content problem; Glob doesn't look inside files.
3a77ff7072:
Wrappers rename things. A retry helper, a package re-export under another name, and an assignment alias all hide the original from a single search. Iterating over discovered names reaches the real entry points in a handful of targeted searches.

A is the wrong tool for content. B doesn't scale, and fills the context with noise. D can't know your repository.
863bdf01a2: In 04_scope_resolver.py, add a headers field to the local orders entry. Confirm that the project entry's Authorization header is still not used. Then explain why the fix for "my override lost its auth header" is to copy the whole entry.
437725927e: In orders_server.py, add a resource catalog://glossary/{term} template and a one-line mention in the server instructions. Re-run example 10 twice: with the explorer unchanged, and with a third agent that reads the glossary for every question. When does a catalogue stop paying off?
6991d2d57c: Optional, with an API key and Claude Code installed: add orders_server.py to a scratch repo with claude mcp add --scope project --transport stdio orders -- python orders_server.py. Run claude mcp list and /mcp, approve the server, and ask for the status of ORD-118204. Compare with the scripted trace in example 16.
f08d4a099f:
Done when you can do all of these:

  • draw the host/client/server picture and the lifecycle from memory;
  • say in one sentence what each scope is for, and which one wins;
  • write a .mcp.json with expansion and no secrets;
  • explain why a thin MCP description loses to Grep, and how to fix it;
  • choose between Grep, Glob, Read, Write and Edit for any request;
  • trace a function through renames without a single-name search.
